title: Does Being Too Nice Cause Misbehavior?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin directly challenges the popular teaching advice that sternness produces better classroom behavior, arguing instead that being nice actually makes classroom management easier, not harder. He lays out five specific mechanisms by which kindness helps: it makes a teacher more likable, which triggers the Law of Reciprocity so students want to behave in return; it deepens accountability because students without a reason to resent the teacher blame themselves instead; it creates leverage, since students value their relationship with a kind teacher more than they fear a consequence; it removes classroom tension that would otherwise fuel excitability; and it eliminates the desire for revenge that drives much of the misbehavior aimed at stern teachers. His crucial caveat is that niceness alone doesn't work -- it must be paired with a consistently enforced classroom management plan, or a pushover teacher will still be overrun regardless of temperament.
points: Kindness triggers the Law of Reciprocity, making students naturally want to return good behavior for a teacher's good treatment.
Without a reason to resent the teacher, misbehaving students are left to blame only themselves, which is the actual mechanism of accountability.
A calm, kind teacher removes classroom tension, and tension is a direct driver of student excitability and misbehavior.
Much student misbehavior functions as quiet revenge against a stern teacher, which kindness short-circuits before it starts.
Niceness only works as a strategy when paired with a classroom management plan that is followed consistently -- otherwise a kind pushover is trampled all the same.
quotes: The idea that being too nice is the reason you’re struggling with classroom management is a misunderstanding of why students misbehave.
The truth is, being nice makes classroom management easier, not harder.
When students like you, they naturally want to listen and behave for you. This is called the Law of Reciprocity.
When you refuse to create friction and resentment with students, they won’t fault you for their misbehavior. They’ll point the finger at themselves, where it belongs.
Much of student misbehavior is revenge on a stern teacher they don’t like. If ever you feel you’re on one side and your students are on the other, then you will struggle with behavior.
The big caveat is that niceness only works when you have an effective classroom management plan that you follow as written.
